newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - London yuppies lift spirits of port wine.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - London yuppies lift spirits of port wine.

text.p: David Delaforce's family has been in the port wine business since 1834 and yet most of his newest customers weren't even born when some of his most popular brands were produced.
Reversing traditional trends, the 25-44 age group is now the fastest growing market in Britain and accounts for 35 percent of the 12 million bottles that are imbibed annually, industry sources say.
Young, urban professionals, buoyed by a vibrant British economy and a strong pound, have tapped into the sweet and fruity port wine because of its prestige and upmarket status, they say.

The rising investment value of vintage port -- the flagship of each producer in Portugal -- changing drinking habits and an aggressive marketing push by the port industry have also boosted sales in Britain.

"After going through severe economic recession, two world wars this century, and a Portuguese revolution in 1974...I think the last decade has been the longest continuous growth in the port wine industry for some years," said Delaforce, who is also chairman of Britain's Port Wine Trade Committee.

Port must still contend with an age-old reputation for giving wicked hangovers and of being the tipple of choice for older aristocrats who would pass the bottle clockwise around the dinner table to ward off the devil's temptations, as one myth goes.
PORT RENAISSANCE
But the lawyers, brokers and other young executives pouring into tastings across the city are testament to a renaissance of port and the long history connecting Britain and Portugal.
The monks of Lamego first made port in the 17th century when the northern part of Portugal was demarcated for its favourable growing conditions.
British demand was uncorked after France slapped high taxes on Bordeaux wines and England's King Charles II retaliated by boycotting all claret imports.

The Metheun Treaty was eventually signed by Britain and Portugal for favourable tariffs after merchants discovered the wines of the Douro Valley in northern Portugal through an English colony in Oporto.
Today, most port is aged in Oporto which enjoys a cool sea breeze and is the home of the Port Wine Institute, the industry's regulatory body. Many of the shippers based there are British-owned.
Port's flavour comes from halting the fermentation process, which retains the sugar, and adding spirits.
CONSUMERS UPGRADE WITH RISING INCOMES

The British market accounts for about 10 percent of world demand but 40 percent of its sales is for the more expensive or premium bottles, raising its dollar value to 15 percent, industry watchers say.

British consumption has been growing at two to four percent a year but exports to Britain from Portugal, the sole producer of port, jumped 17 percent in January from a year ago, according to the Port Wine Institute.

"The main people who are drinking port are between 25 and 44 years old in the U.K. and the reason is that it is linked with prestige and lifestyle, which we are not trying to discourage," said Sue Glasgow, spokeswoman for the institute in London.
"At the moment the interest in port is coming back because people have more disposable income and they will spend their money on port," she said.

Delaforce, whose son is a winemaker and blender in Oporto, said port has overtaken cognac worldwide in sales, helped by a lower alcohol content and a trend toward drinking more at home. Only 25 percent of port sales are at restaurants.

"Overall the industry worldwide is growing but the major part is in Europe, and obviously the U.K., and North America," said Delaforce, whose brands are now owned by International Distillers and Vintners (IDV), the drinks business arm of Grand Metropolitan Plc.
Portugal drinks about 1.3 million cases a year of port wine even though it has a population about one-fifth that of Britain, so Britain's growth potential is promising, he said.
VINTAGE PORT SOLD TO THE HIGHEST BIDDERS

Paul Bowker, head of the wine department at Christies International, said the most expensive bottle of vintage port it sold recently was a 1931 Quinta do Noval for about 550 pounds ($893), nearly double what it would have fetched a few years ago.

"The port market over the last five years got into a low situation where there was not much demand and prices were flat," he said. "In the last couple of years we have seen a great improvement in that... think people realised it was getting too cheap."

Vintage wines, which account for only three to four percent of total production, are the only types of port that are bought as investments since the others do not age in bottles. And because port is produced only in Portugal, and certified by the institute, there is a limit as to how much is produced.
"The investment value of a vintage port is a good one...because of the limitation on the amount of port they can make," Glasgow said.
A vintage bottle selling for 12-15 pounds three years ago is now offered at 20-30 pounds, Bowker said.
Robust international demand and undervalued, older wines have also fuelled higher prices in vintage port.
"Historically it's been a very good investment but a very long-term investment for 10-15 years," he said. "Only in recent years has the value of port increased so much, by 10 percent or doubled."

Industry officials also believe that other types of port, such as the orange-coloured tawny port that can be aged in wood for up to 40 years and can cost from eight to 40 pounds, represents good value when measured against other wines aged for so long.
FEEDING THE KITCHEN MORE THAN THE CLIENTS

Port wine sellers still have obstacles, including the tendency to drink port only in cold weather -- 40 percent of British are in the weeks leading up to Christmas -- or only after meals and not as an aperitif.
But a socially conscious public that drinks more at home and drives less, and orders less-spirited drinks when out on the town, should favour port.

Stephen Dallyn, president of Winetrails, which offers customised food and wine holidays, said there is a trend toward upmarket "gourmet" trips that would naturally be favoured by the scores of British tourists visiting Portugal.

"If you accept the premise that wine travel is growing across Europe and accept it is a high quality product...then I think it will be inevitable that there will be continued growth, especially coupled with the fact there is a strong historical connection between the Douro and port and the U.K.," he said.
But back at home, even the restaurants are having a hard time pouring more port for their customers.

At Leith's restaurant in an 18th century townhouse in the Notting Hill district of London, managing director Nick Tarayan said his customers are choosing after-dinner drinks that have even less alcohol than port, such as a sweet champagne.

"I think it has more competition now than it ever has had," he said, while pointing to his chef's desire to use port in his sauces. "We actually serve more to the kitchen than to the clients." ($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
